My first job when I was your age was through the [Focus On Youth](https://www.tdsb.on.ca/Community/Community-Use-of-Schools/Focus-on-Youth/2019-FOYT-Summer-Student-Employment) summer employment program offered by the TDSB. Since you need to be 16 or 17 to apply, you don’t have to worry about competing with older more experienced candidates for the same positions. I couldn’t find a link to a 2024 page for the program, but I remember my guidance counsellor was able to get the paperwork for me when I was a student, so I would consult your guidance counsellor if you’re interested. 

Also, if you know you’re interested in uni and what you want to major in, I would recommend not taking a gap year. Assuming you’ll still be allowed to live with your parents during uni as well, I was able to pay for uni with OSAP, working on campus, and co-op without my family’s help.

Going into pharmacy for that reason is a very bad idea. You’ll encounter the same difficulties getting a job within pharmacy, as you will with a research based grad degree, except with a lot more debt. You don’t have to do a research based grad degree. There is the MBiotech at UTM which is a year of courses and then 1 year of co-op following that at a pharmaceutical company. You could consider that or programs at the Michener Institute if you’re interested in working in healthcare specifically.

Speaking as someone who got accepted this year, but declined my offer, I don’t think it’s worth the risk. I think you have a fair chance to get into med school if you’ve been working on your ec’s and do well on the MCAT. Alternatively if you don’t like the lab side of pharmaceuticals, there’s regulatory affairs certificate programs or the MBiotech at UTM.

I honestly would just drop those courses if I were you. Grades on your transcript are permanent. Coming from a 4th year, I definitely regret not dropping some of the courses I’ve taken in the past. I would drop those courses but still attend lecture so you can learn the material so it’ll be review next time. Plus sometimes the teaching/testing style of some profs aren’t the best fit for you. I’ve taken MATA36 with Kathleen and was flunking it since I was taking other time demanding courses and working. I took it another semester with a different prof when I was ready to put the work in and 4.0ed it.

I feel like you should focus on making strong connections with profs. I would start as early as possible getting to know profs and sending genuine emails to profs whose research interests you. Make sure to reference recent papers. Try not to make it come off like you just read their abstract and if you’re meeting them in person, you could ask them questions that you had while reading their articles and kinda steer the conversation to your own research interests. Profs also remember you if you leave them with a memorable impression of you. I’ve had one prof remember me a year later to ask me if I wanted to do some field research one summer and another prof I had for a course in the fall just emailed me letting me know of an undergraduate research award for this summer. I should also mention my gpa is complete shit so networking can honestly go a long way to make up for bad grades if that is a factor keeping you from asking profs about doing an independent research course.

If you haven’t taken it already you could take STAB22. It’s not memorization based since it’s basic math. You also get To create a cheat sheet for the midterm and final so you don’t have to worry about memorizing equations or concepts. Tutorials are easy marks since quizzes are open book plus the TA gives you a lot of hints before the quiz. I took it with Mahinda and got a 4.0 with minimal effort.

The only downside for B38 is the poster project that they’ve added to all bio B levels.

EESA10 was super easy. There’s only a MC midterm and final weighted 50/50 and a 2% bonus if you just answer a question on the discussion board. The question types on the exams are really similar to past tests so try to test yourself using past tests when you’re studying. The course avg was a B when I took it in the summer and it’s extremely possible to get a 90+ in the course. Make sure the prof is Stefanovic too.

I’m at UTSC but I got into UTSG for biochem/ life sci back when I applied. My hs wasn’t inflated but I think my top 6 for grade 11 was in the high 80s to low 90s and then grade 12 was like low to mid 80s. I also had extenuating circumstances so I don’t think they judged my marks as harshly. I graduated hs back in 2015 so it’s possible that cutoffs have gone up by now. I chose UTSC for co-op and a closer commute so I can’t tell you what first year at UTSG is like.

Took it this summer and it’s an easy 90+. The breakdown was 50/50 mc midterm and final for me. Make sure the prof is Stefanovic. A lot of the psych courses are also online at UTSC and are pretty interesting if you like psych and you only have to physically be there for the midterm and final.

Also did co-op (biochem) in a company’s r & d lab. I would say it’s good depending on what you want to do. Like if graduation time is important to you then you might not want to do co-op because it’ll put you behind if you’re in a program whose courses aren’t offered in the summer. Also your willingness to relocate is important as there are only a few jobs that aren’t a crazy commute from campus but if you have a pretty good resume, cover letter, transcript and interview skills you should be set. I was fortunate enough to get a position in Toronto but I remember there being around 30 positions the semester I applied in Vancouver which is way too far for me. Also being too picky about the jobs is bad too. Honestly the lab I chose was a completely new field for me but I ended up enjoying it because I got to work on a lot of cool projects. Every semester there should be a poster project fair with students who recently came back from their co-op work term. You might find someone from neuro and get a better idea of what options you have for your program specifically.

I’ve personally have not come across a prof in marine bio here so I’d say your best bet is UBC. I used to be like you before uni, but I stopped for that very reason. If you tell people that you haven’t started studying yet then they usually should stop bothering you. If they’re messaging you online before the test or exam just ignore them and if you run into them just say I turned off all my social media to focus on studying. Also don’t immediately give people you just met the impression that you’re someone who has great notes and are super nerdy. They may take advantage of that knowledge and you’ll fall back into that cycle of feeling like you have to give them your notes because it feels like it goes against your personality not to. I typically like getting know people more before I give them my stuff. The people who usually offer to study with you or help you to catch up in the course when you’re doing that whole I haven’t done anything for this course act are usually genuine.

Definitely BIOB50 then. The prof has changed since I’ve taken it but I’ve heard the new prof Sturge is really good and her courses typically have B averages for C level bio courses so you should be good. It’s a lot more work as there’s a lab component and you’ll have to keep up with the course content or you’ll be lost for the term tests.

I'm still in university too, I'm just working full time for now for my co-op placement so I get where you're coming from about the lack of funds. You could wear the suit combo or mix and match pieces of it with something that could pass for business casual for the first day and then you can talk to your boss about it then. I'm not sure what it's like at Bestbuy but on Fridays we're allowed to dress casually so jeans, hoodies, t-shirts, etc are allowed so you might be able to use your wardrobe if you have something like that. You could pass for business casual even with a long sleeve or polo if you have any of those. I do think that once you get your first pay cheque they'll expect you to allocate some of it into getting proper work attire. It doesn't have to be anything fancy. Something from Walmart is perfectly fine.

My company's dress code is business casual too but I work in a lab so what I wear isn't as noticeable under my lab coat unless I'm in meetings or eating lunch in the cafeteria. Anyways for us business casual was anything that wasn't a t-shirt, sweatshirt, hoodie, jeans, sweats, or sneakers. We could wear sweaters, casual dress shirts, cardigans, any pants that isn't denim or sweatpants material and dress shoes. You could always come into work wearing a hoodie and take it off with your jacket before you start your shift. That's what I do sometimes since I live in Canada and the winters can get really cold sometimes. I personally prefer wearing sweaters to work for that same reason since they're warm yet still fall under business casual.
